name: Samsing
tagline: Tea slopes where the Dooars meet Neora Valley
meta_description: Samsing guide: tea garden village at 900 m above the Dooars, Rocky Island, Mouchuki, Neora Valley walks, homestays, costs and how to reach from Siliguri.
summary: Samsing is a tea garden village at about 900 m in the first hills above Chalsa, on the southern edge of Neora Valley National Park. It is cooler than the plains, a one-hour drive from Murti and Lataguri, and the base for Rocky Island, Suntalekhola and forest walks.

local_story.title: Bhutan's hills, Britain's tea, Gorkha homes
paras: Until 1865 these hills east of the Teesta were Bhutanese territory. The British took them in the Duar War, and a few kilometres west, above Gorubathan, the ruins of Daling fort still mark one of the Bhutanese strongholds they stormed. Under the Treaty of Sinchula the slopes became part of British India and were handed to planters, who cleared forest for tea on the cooler ridges above the plains.

The gardens were worked largely by Nepali-speaking families who came over the hills from Nepal and Darjeeling, and Samsing today is a Gorkha village with a tea factory, garden lines, a market, a school and a Hindu temple. Administratively it belonged to Darjeeling district's Kalimpong subdivision until February 2017, when Kalimpong became a district of its own.

Above the village the tea stops and Neora Valley National Park begins, one of the least disturbed forests in West Bengal, declared in 1986. Samsing's homestays and the forest corporation's camps make it the cheapest way to sleep beside that forest.

did_you_know: Samsing is administered as part of Kalimpong district, created on 14 February 2017, even though most visitors reach it through the Dooars plains via Chalsa.
Neora Valley National Park, on Samsing's doorstep, covers about 88 km² and rises to over 3,000 m; it is one of West Bengal's red panda strongholds.
The hills around Samsing were Bhutanese until the Treaty of Sinchula in November 1865, which ended the Duar War.
intro: Climb out of Chalsa and within half an hour the heat of the plains is behind you. The road winds through Metali and into tea, and Samsing appears on a ridge with the garden falling away on every side and the forest of Neora Valley above. On clear winter mornings you look south over the Dooars plain all the way to the haze.

Samsing is not a sight in itself; it is a place to slow down. Walk the garden roads, visit Rocky Island on the Murti, take the forest corporation's path towards Mouchuki or go on to the hanging bridge at Suntalekhola. Homestays here are cheaper than in Lataguri, and nights are pleasantly cool even in April.

highlights.title: Tea garden roads
highlights.text: Samsing's garden spreads across the ridge, with paths between sections and views over the plains. Walk out at 7 am in the plucking season and you share the road with workers heading to the bushes.

highlights.title: Rocky Island on the Murti
highlights.text: A few kilometres below Samsing, the Murti runs through a valley of huge boulders. Rocky Island is a riverside camping spot where you can sit by the water or stay in a tent.

highlights.title: Mouchuki and the forest edge
highlights.text: The forest corporation's Mouchuki camp lies above the village towards Neora Valley. The walk up gives views and good birding on the forest edge.

highlights.title: Suntalekhola's hanging bridge
highlights.text: Five kilometres on, the orange stream comes out of the forest under a suspension footbridge, with forest cottages on the far side. An easy half-day or an overnight.

highlights.title: Cool nights above the plains
highlights.text: At about 900 m, Samsing is several degrees cooler than Lataguri. Winter nights can drop to around 8–10 °C, so bring a fleece.

how_to_reach.text: From NJP or Bagdogra about 85–95 km via Sevoke, Malbazar, Chalsa and Metali, two and a half to three hours, ₹3,500–4,500.
Bus from Siliguri to Malbazar or Chalsa, ₹100–150, then a shared jeep or local service to Metali and Samsing, ₹40–80. Jeeps leave when full, mostly in the morning.
About 20–40 km, 45 minutes to an hour by car via Chalsa, ₹1,200–1,800 one way. Many visitors come for the day.

where_to_stay: Samsing has family homestays in and around the village, typically ₹1,200–1,800 per person with dinner and breakfast, and a few private resorts on the roads towards Rocky Island and Suntalekhola. The forest corporation runs the Samsing Eco Tourism Centre and the small Mouchuki camp above the village, and the Suntaleykhola Eco-Tourism Centre and river camp 5 km further on. Rocky Island has a private riverside camp with tents and cottages; check current status, as river camps close for the monsoon.
tips: Start from Siliguri by 9 am; the hill road above Metali is narrow and slow behind trucks.
Carry a warm layer even in spring; evenings at 900 m are cool.
Bring cash; Samsing's shops take UPI when the signal holds, which is not always.
Walk garden roads only in daylight and with care near the forest edge.
Avoid June to September, when slides close the road and the rivers rise; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Morning walk through Samsing tea garden
experiences.summary: Samsing's tea garden covers the ridge and slopes around the village, with views over the plains. A morning walk on the estate roads shows hill tea at about 900 m, between the Dooars' flat gardens and Darjeeling's steep ones.
body: Samsing sits in a transition zone. Below, in the Dooars, tea grows on flat land under tall shade trees and goes mostly into CTC. Above, in Darjeeling, it clings to steep slopes and becomes orthodox leaf tea. Samsing's bushes grow on rolling ridges in between, with shade trees and drains cut along the contours, and the forest of Neora Valley above.

Walk out early, when pluckers head to the sections and the light comes low across the bushes. Ask your homestay host which roads are open to walkers and which sections are being plucked or sprayed that day. If someone from the garden walks with you, ask about the work: how much leaf a plucker picks in a day, how the rains change the flush, how life in the lines has changed.

The garden is a workplace and private land. Keep to estate roads, ask before photographing anyone and do not enter the factory without permission. In winter the bushes are pruned and the garden is quiet, but the views over the plains are clearer.

faqs.q: Can we visit the Samsing tea factory?
faqs.a: There is no fixed public tour. Some visitors are shown around on request in the manufacturing season, roughly March to November, depending on the garden's work. Ask your homestay, who may know the staff. Never walk into the factory unannounced.

faqs.q: What kind of tea does Samsing make?
faqs.a: Gardens in this belt mostly produce CTC and some orthodox tea for the Indian and export market. It is not sold under the Darjeeling name, which is protected for registered Darjeeling gardens. Ask locally for garden tea to take home.

faqs.q: When do pluckers work in Samsing?
faqs.a: Plucking runs from about March to November, with the busiest months in the spring and monsoon flushes. Work usually starts early in the morning. From December to February bushes are pruned and rested, so there is little plucking.

experiences.title: Rocky Island and the Murti boulders
experiences.summary: Below Samsing the Murti runs through a narrow valley strewn with house-sized boulders. Rocky Island is a riverside spot with a private camp where you can picnic, sit on the rocks or sleep in a tent to the sound of the water.
body: Rocky Island lies a few kilometres from Samsing on the Murti, which here is still a mountain river, clear and fast, squeezed between forest and huge granite boulders. A private camp on the bank offers tents and simple rooms, and day visitors come for picnics and photographs on the rocks.

The river is beautiful and dangerous. Currents between boulders are strong, the rocks are slippery, and water levels rise quickly after rain upstream in Neora Valley. Do not swim, keep children close and leave the bank at once if the water colour changes. In winter, people sit for hours on the warm stones with tea; that is the right way to use the place.

If you stay overnight, the campfire, the stars and the roar of the river make a fine night. Ask the camp about current rates, food and toilets, and check current status before you travel, as river camps close during the monsoon and after flood damage.

faqs.q: How far is Rocky Island from Samsing?
faqs.a: A few kilometres, about 15–20 minutes by car down a narrow road towards the Murti. Many visitors combine Rocky Island and Suntalekhola in a half-day by car for roughly ₹1,500–2,000 from Samsing. You can also walk if you are fit, though the return is uphill.

faqs.q: Can we swim at Rocky Island?
faqs.a: No. The Murti runs fast between boulders here, with strong currents and sudden rises after rain in the hills. People have drowned in rivers like this. Sit on the rocks, paddle in a shallow edge only if locals say it is safe, and keep children well back.

faqs.q: Is camping at Rocky Island safe?
faqs.a: The private camp is set back from the main channel and closes during the monsoon. Follow the staff's instructions, do not walk on the rocks after dark and keep your tent zipped. Ask about the weather; if heavy rain is forecast, sleep in a room rather than a tent.

experiences.title: Walk up to Mouchuki on the forest edge
experiences.summary: Above Samsing a road and path climb towards Mouchuki, where the forest corporation has a small camp at the edge of Neora Valley National Park. The walk gives wide views over the Dooars and good forest-edge birding.
body: Neora Valley National Park, declared in 1986, covers about 88 km² of forest from the foothills above Samsing to ridges over 3,000 m near Rachela. The lower park, near Samsing, is warm broadleaf forest; the upper park holds rhododendron, bamboo and red pandas. Most of the park is closed to casual walking, but the edge above Samsing can be explored with a guide.

The walk to Mouchuki climbs steadily through tea and then forest-edge scrub, with views opening over the plains and back to the Murti valley. Birds are the main wildlife: barbets, sunbirds, laughingthrushes, minivets and, with luck, hornbills. Leeches appear after rain, so wear long socks.

Go with a local guide, who will know which paths are open and where you may not enter the park without permission. Forest department rules on entry into Neora Valley change; check current status before you travel. Carry water and snacks, since there are no shops beyond the village.

faqs.q: Can we enter Neora Valley National Park from Samsing?
faqs.a: Entry into the park needs forest department permission and usually a guide, and many areas are closed to visitors. From Samsing, the common walks stay along the park's edge, such as towards Mouchuki. Ask the forest office or your guide and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How hard is the walk to Mouchuki?
faqs.a: Moderate: a steady climb of a few hundred metres on road and path, taking three to four hours return at an easy pace with stops. Shoes with grip are needed. Anyone used to walking an hour or two uphill will manage.

faqs.q: Are there red pandas near Samsing?
faqs.a: Red pandas live in Neora Valley's upper forests, well above Samsing, generally above 2,000 m. You will not see them on the lower walks. Lava and the upper Neora Valley, in the Kalimpong land, are the places to try, with a guide and patience.

experiences.title: Gundruk, squash and a Samsing homestay meal
experiences.summary: Samsing's Nepali-speaking homestay families cook hill food: rice, dal, squash, local greens, fermented gundruk, chicken curry and hot pickles. Ask to sit in the kitchen while dinner is made; it is the best cooking class in the Dooars.
body: Hill kitchens in Samsing are built around the rice pot and what grows in the garden. Iskus (chayote squash) appears in almost every meal, along with mustard greens, beans and potatoes. Gundruk, fermented and dried leafy greens, goes into a sour soup in winter. Pickles of radish, chilli and tomato add heat, and dalle chillies, small and fierce, sit on the side.

Meat is usually chicken or pork, and in some homes there will be dried meat or local cheese. Breakfast may bring sel roti, a ring-shaped fried rice bread, especially around festivals. Tea comes strong and milky, and some families will make a glass of black garden tea if you ask.
Tell your hosts early if you are vegetarian or avoid chillies; they will adjust. Ask if you can watch or help in the kitchen, and ask about the names of dishes; families are usually proud to explain.

faqs.q: What is gundruk?
faqs.a: Gundruk is a fermented and dried leafy green, usually from mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, made in Nepali households of the Himalaya. It is cooked into a sour soup or pickle, especially in winter. It tastes tangy and earthy and goes well with rice.

faqs.q: Is homestay food in Samsing spicy?
faqs.a: Pickles and chilli sauces can be very hot, especially dalle chillies, but main dishes are moderate. Tell your hosts how much heat you like; they are used to guests from the plains and abroad. Children's meals can be made without chilli.

faqs.q: Are meals included in Samsing homestays?
faqs.a: Most homestays include dinner and breakfast in their per-person rate, about ₹1,200–1,800 in 2025–26. Lunch is extra, about ₹150–250, and should be ordered in the morning. Confirm what is included when you book.

faqs.q: Where is Samsing?
faqs.a: Samsing is a tea garden village at about 900 m in the hills above Chalsa, on the southern edge of Neora Valley National Park. It is administered as part of Kalimpong district but reached through the Dooars, about 85–95 km from Siliguri via Malbazar and Chalsa.

faqs.q: Is Samsing worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want cool air, tea gardens and river valleys close to the Dooars parks. It is quiet, cheap and an hour from Murti and Lataguri. It is not for sightseeing checklists; come to walk, sit by the Murti and sleep well.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Samsing?
faqs.a: One or two nights. One night covers a tea garden walk, Rocky Island and Suntalekhola. Two nights add the walk towards Mouchuki and a slower pace. Combine with two nights in Murti or Lataguri for safaris.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Samsing?
faqs.a: October to April. Winter mornings are clear with views over the plains, and spring brings green tea and warm days. May is warm but fine. June to September brings heavy rain, slides on the road from Metali and swollen rivers.

faqs.q: How much does a Samsing homestay cost?
faqs.a: Family homestays charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person a night with dinner and breakfast in 2025–26. Forest corporation cottages in the area run about ₹2,000–3,000 a room. Private resorts on the river roads cost more.

faqs.q: Can we see wildlife in Samsing?
faqs.a: Mostly birds, with occasional barking deer and, rarely, elephants in the lower forest. Leopards are present but seldom seen. For large mammals, go down to Gorumara and Chapramari. Samsing's strength is birding along the forest edge.

faqs.q: Is there public transport to Samsing?
faqs.a: Buses run from Siliguri to Malbazar and Chalsa, and shared jeeps go on to Samsing a few times a day, mostly in the morning. It works for budget travellers with time. Families usually hire a car.

faqs.q: Is Samsing safe in the monsoon?
faqs.a: The road above Metali sees landslides and the rivers rise fast in heavy rain, so we avoid June to September. If you go, travel in daylight, keep a buffer day and do not go near the Murti or Suntalekhola when they are high. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Does Samsing have ATMs and mobile network?
faqs.a: Mobile signal is fair in the village for Jio and Airtel and weak in the valleys. ATMs are unreliable, so carry cash from Siliguri or Malbazar. UPI works where data does.
